title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
The page states Euler's version of Lagrange's integral of the separated equation dx/sqrt(X) ± dy/sqrt(Y) = 0. Here X = A+Bx+Cx^2+Dx^3+Ex^4, Y is the same quartic in y, and K is the same quartic in k. The constant is fixed by the condition that y=0 gives x=k.

Theorem IV (sec. 52). For dx/sqrt(X) - dy/sqrt(Y) = 0 the integral is
[2A + B(x+y) + 2Cxy + Dxy(x+y) + 2Ex^2y^2 + 2sqrt(XY)]/(x-y)^2 = [2A + Bk + 2sqrt(AK)]/k^2.
For the + sign, sqrt(Y) changes sign, so sqrt(XY) becomes -sqrt(XY) in the numerator and sqrt(AK) becomes -sqrt(AK) in the constant.

In modern terms this is the first integral that Lagrange obtained with his auxiliary time t and his p=x+y, q=x-y device. One can write it as
(sqrt(X)+sqrt(Y))^2/(x-y)^2 - E(x+y)^2 - D(x+y) = const.
Expanding: X+Y-[E(x+y)^2+D(x+y)](x-y)^2 = 2A + B(x+y) + C(x^2+y^2) + Dxy(x+y) + 2Ex^2y^2. Euler's 2Cxy differs from C(x^2+y^2) by C(x-y)^2, which only shifts the constant. Setting y=0, x=k gives the stated right-hand side. This is the algebraic form of the addition theorem for elliptic integrals of the first kind.

Corollary I (sec. 53). Putting D=E=0 recovers the quadratic case of Theorem III in a second form.
- From Theorem III, 2sqrt(XY) = 2sqrt(A(A+Bk+Ck^2)) - B(k-x-y) + 2Cxy; this rearrangement is verified.
- Comparing the two forms lets the radical be eliminated.
- Substituting gives, on the next page, a rational relation. It leads to Euler's canonical symmetric biquadratic α + 2β(x+y) + γ(x^2+y^2) + 2δxy = 0.

Purpose: the 'Dilucidationes' (E506) re-derive and clarify Lagrange's method. They give explicit closed forms of the constant of integration and show how the earlier results (Theorems II, III) arise as special cases.
errors: The first displayed integral (minus-sign case) is printed with denominator (x+y)^2; it must be (x-y)^2. Test case X=Y=1 gives dx-dy=0, i.e. x-y constant, which (2+2)/(x-y)^2 = const reproduces. Corollary I itself uses (x-y)^2. This is a typographical error.
In the plus-sign case the constant is printed as (2A+Bk-2sqrt(Ak))/kk; it should be sqrt(AK) with capital K (the quartic value), as in the first case.
The sign convention matters. dx/sqrt(X) + dy/sqrt(Y) = 0 differs from the minus case only by the branch of sqrt(Y), so both formulas are one statement. Euler treats them as two, which is not wrong.

ideas.what: Algebraic first integral of dx/sqrt(X) = ± dy/sqrt(Y) for a general quartic X, normalised by y=0 ↔ x=k
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange addition theorem for elliptic integrals of the first kind, in the form of the invariant (sqrt X + sqrt Y)^2/(x-y)^2 - E(x+y)^2 - D(x+y)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1750s, Fagnano-inspired addition theorems); this symmetric form is credited to Lagrange (Turin Miscellanea, 1766–69)
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier papers on the integration of dx/sqrt(X)=dy/sqrt(Y) (e.g. E251, E261) and Institutiones calculi integralis vol. I; restated here in E506

ideas.what: Elimination of the radical by comparing two forms of the integral (quadratic case)
ideas.modern_name: Rational symmetric biquadratic relation, Euler's canonical equation α+2β(x+y)+γ(x²+y²)+2δxy=0
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on the canonical biquadratic and Institutiones calculi integralis; continued on the following page of E506

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful restatement of a well-known result: Lagrange's symmetric integral of the elliptic differential equation, with Euler's explicit constant. Its reduction to the quadratic case is standard and fully documented in the history of elliptic addition theorems. The only noteworthy items are misprints.
transcription_corrections: First integral: the transcription faithfully records the printed '(x+y)^2', but the mathematically correct denominator is (x-y)^2 (printing error in the original).
Second constant: the print and transcription read '2√Ak'; it should be '2√(AK)'.
